Hormuz Oil Flows Unlikely to Return to Pre-War Levels, Rystad Says
The United States and Iran could reach some form of a limited agreement by the middle of 2027, which would allow oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz to continue to gradually recover, but fundamental differences will remain, and the Middle East situation will remain far from normal next year, according to Rystad Energy.
"Achieving a comprehensive settlement would require addressing issues related to Iran's nuclear program, sanctions, Tehran-backed armed groups in the region, and the security of maritime shipping, while also taking into account Israel's security interests," Rystad Energy said in a report cited by Azeri news agency Trend .
"We consider it unlikely that all these points of contention can be resolved within the coming year," the analysts led by Rystad's Head of Geopolitical Analysis, Jorge León, wrote in the report.
Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz will continue to recover gradually, but are unlikely to reach pre-war levels in a normalized trade flow, according to the energy intelligence firm.
Rystad Energy has estimated that crude oil exports from Persian Gulf producers averaged nearly 12 million barrels per day (bpd) in September and the first 20 days of October.
"While this is well above the lows recorded earlier in the conflict, it remains substantially below the pre-war level of approximately 18 million barrels per day," the report reads.
While flows have recovered substantially from the lows in the spring, the security situation in and near the Strait of Hormuz has actually deteriorated, with a higher number of attacks on tankers in recent weeks, according to Rystad Energy.
In the near term, the risk of renewed military escalation following the U.S. midterm elections could be another setback to the recovering Hormuz oil flows.
Early on Tuesday, as voting in the midterms began on the U.S. East Coast, oil prices rebounded from Monday's 7% loss following a Wall Street Journal report about a U.S. strike on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Japan faces diplomatic dilemma amid joint pressure from nuclear neighbors As the Ukraine war grinds on, ties between Russia and neighboring Japan are at their worst in decades. Tokyo wants more support from Washington, but some Japanese are concerned they may not get it.
Japan faces diplomatic dilemma amid joint pressure from nuclear neighbors
< iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6012016/nx-s1-9990133" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
As the Ukraine war grinds on, ties between Russia and neighboring Japan are at their worst in decades. Tokyo wants more support from Washington, but some Japanese are concerned they may not get it.
AILSA CHANG, HOST: And now to Russia's war in Ukraine. This war has raised tensions not only in Europe but also in Asia. Ties between Russia and neighboring Japan are at their worst in decades. Tokyo would like more support from Washington, but as NPR's Anthony Kuhn reports, some Japanese people are concerned they may not get it. ANTHONY KUHN, BYLINE: In a video released by Russia's federal security bureau, FSB agents charge into a hotel room on Sakhalin Island in Russia's Far East on October 13. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED FSB AGENT: (Non-English language spoken). YUKI IMAI: (Non-English language spoken). KUHN: The agents pin Japanese journalist Yuki Imai to the ground and handcuff him. They question him and take him to Moscow to face trial on charges of espionage. Japan's government denies the charges. The FSB says Imai was reporting on soldiers from Russia's Far East who were deployed to Ukraine. Shinji Hyodo, a Russia expert at the National Institute for Defense Studies in Tokyo, argues that the journalist was just doing his job. SHINJI HYODO: (Through interpreter) I believe the Russian side intends to use this as a political bargaining chip to exert pressure on Japan. KUHN: Hyodo says that underlying the current tensions are Japan's sanctions on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine. Russia now sees Japan as hostile, and bilateral relations have gone into a tailspin. HYODO: (Through interpreter) I think it's fair to say that Japan is currently facing its greatest diplomatic challenge since the end of the war. This is no longer just a bilateral issue between Japan and Russia. KUHN: There's also what Hyodo calls the China factor. China has been putting pressure on Japan since last year, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said that a Chinese blockade of Taiwan could justify a Japanese military response. Russia relies on China's support in its war on Ukraine, and it's joined China in pressuring Japan. Another factor is a long-running territorial dispute between Russia and Japan. (SOUNDBITE OF FACTORY MACHINERY) KUHN: In August, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited a seafood factory, hospital and school on his first visit to one of four disputed islands called the Southern Kurils by Russia and the Northern Territories by Japan. The Soviet Union seized the islands at the end of World War II. They never signed a permanent peace treaty because of the dispute and because the U.S. warned them not to. This episode was called the Dulles intervention. James Brown, an expert on Japan-Russia relations at Temple University in Tokyo, explains. JAMES BROWN: This was the suggestion from John Foster Dulles, the secretary of state, in 1956 that if Japan were to make an agreement with the Soviet Union, settling the territorial dispute, well, then perhaps the United States would remain forevermore in holding, administering Okinawa. KUHN: So the Soviet Union kept the islands, and the U.S. returned to Japan the island of Okinawa, which remains a key U.S. military hub in Asia. Brown says Japan's media generally don't mention the U.S.'s role in the territorial dispute so as not to offend its only ally as it faces three nuclear powers - Russia, China and North Korea. BROWN: Japan's situation is essentially they have no Plan B, which means that they have to rely on the United States. They have to flatter the Trump administration. They have to do everything possible to avoid abandonment. KUHN: The U.S. has criticized Russia's arrest of the Japanese journalist, but Shinji Hyodo says that the U.S. generally doesn't seem very interested in Japan's conflict with Russia. And he says Japan is concerned about the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, this month. HYODO: (Through interpreter) There is a possibility that a trilateral summit involving the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia could take place, potentially leading to the U.S. being swayed toward the positions held by China and Russia. KUHN: It's unclear whether Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will meet with either Russian or Chinese leaders at the summit. Anthony Kuhn, NPR News, Seoul. At least seven flights and a cruise ship in Europe received bomb threats, causing disruption at airports although ⁠no devices were discovered. At least two flights to Warsaw, two to Sofia, two to Rome and one to Murcia airport in Spain were subjected to the threats on Tuesday and another flight to Sofia had been threatened a day earlier. ⁠
An airport in Warsaw was briefly ⁠shut and the Italian Air Force ​accompanied one of the flights to Rome , while an Israel-bound cruise ship was searched for bombs in Greece.
Authorities diverted a LOT flight from London that was meant to land at Warsaw’s Chopin airport to nearby Modlin airport, which was closed and then reopened ​after the plane was searched and no device was found. Another Warsaw-bound flight, an ‌SAS flight from Copenhagen, landed at Chopin as ‌scheduled. Chopin airport said no device was found and the airport remained operational.
Bomb threats were made against planes traveling from Milan/Bergamo and Dublin ‌to Sofia, Bulgaria’s transport ministry said in a statement to Reuters. Both landed safely and no explosive devices were found on inspection.
The Bergamo flight was operated by Wizz Air and was carrying 176 passengers, the statement said. The Dublin flight, operated by Ryanair, had 186 passengers on board. Bulgarian news agency BTA had earlier quoted an interior ministry official as saying a flight from Israel had been affected, but authorities later said this was not the case.
In Murcia in southeastern ‌Spain, parts of an airport were cordoned off after a bomb threat was reported on a Ryanair flight from Manchester. Officials said the report proved to be a hoax, and the airport resumed normal operations after authorities found no explosives on board.
Two other Ryanair flights - one from Lisbon and another from Dublin - were searched at Rome’s Fiumicino airport following bomb threats, said a source from airport operator ADR. The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until it landed. The alert was cleared and the airport continued to operate as usual with no effects on other flights, the person said.
An explosives detection dog and a diver searched the Panama-flagged Crown Iris cruise ship on the Greek island of Syros after an unknown person said an explosive device had ⁠been attached to the boat’s hull, authorities said. Initial checks found no explosive device with coast guard specialists expected to carry ​out further inspections before the ship could resume its voyage.
Meanwhile, Czech public media workers went on a one-day strike to protest a government plan to overhaul how public broadcasters are funded. The legislation, led by populist billionaire turned prime minister Andrej Babiš, has been criticised as threatening the independence of the media organisations.
Russia bombarded Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in waves on ⁠Tuesday, knocking out power to swathes of the country with dozens of missiles and hundreds of drones, a week before US-brokered peace talks were due to resume.
At a ​press conference in Berlin with German chancellor Friedrich Merz, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack showed that ‌Moscow was intent on killing people instead of building ‌on the humanitarian ceasefire in and around Oleshky.
Merz warned that the outcome of the war in Ukraine “will determine European security for a long time to come.” He said Germany will be coordinating with France and the UK, and will host a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin later this month.
The European Commission will host ⁠a meeting regarding Ukraine with representatives ⁠from the ⁠United ​States, Ukraine and its key European allies on Wednesday , Commission ⁠spokesperson Paula Pinho said. “So tomorrow the European ⁠Commission will host a ​meeting with representatives ‌from Ukraine, ‌from the United States, France, Germany , ‌the UK, Nato and the World Bank and this meeting will build on earlier talks that took place ‌in Miami,” Pinho told reporters in Brussels.
A bomb threat to an ⁠Israel-bound cruise ship prompted a security operation at the ⁠Greek island port of ⁠Syros after an unknown person claimed ⁠an explosive device had been attached to its hull, Greek authorities said.
The ⁠Panama-flagged Crown Iris was due ​to sail ‌to Haifa carrying ‌940 passengers and 597 crew ‌members when the threat was received, Reuters reported.
Coast guard personnel assisted by an explosives detection dog and a private diver searched the vessel, while ‌a special coast guard unit was deployed to the scene.
Initial ​checks found no explosive device. Coast guard specialists are expected to arrive at 9.30pm (7.30pm GMT) ⁠to carry out further inspections before the ​ship ​can resume its voyage.
Here are some images from earlier today as Czech public media workers went on a one-day strike to protest a government plan to overhaul how public broadcasters are funded.
The legislation, led by populist billionaire turned prime minister Andrej Babiš, has been criticised as threatening the independence of the media organisations. The plan led to street protests in Prague last month.
Employees of Czech Television holding a banner reading 'Strike' march in front of the broadcaster's headquarters in Prague, Czechia. Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television would be financed from the state budget, not from an existing system of regular fees from individuals, households and businesses. The media would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could likely lead to staff layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.
Demonstrators gather at Wenceslas Square in Prague, Czechia, 03 November 2026, during a nationwide walkout by staff of public service broadcasters Czech Television and Czech Radio. Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA Critics say the overhaul would give the ruling three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under prime minister Robert Fico and in Hungary before former prime minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
Michal Kubal, chief news editor at Czech Television, said the strike today is unprecedented in the history of Czech public service media.
Public gathering in support of Czech Television employees during a strike by Czech public television and radio workers against government plans to cut financing and move funding to the state budget. Photograph: Eva Kořínková/Reuters On their TV screens, Czech residents on Tuesday saw an announcement saying:
We are doing everything we can to ensure that we can continue to provide a public service in its full scope and quality in the future.
Demonstrators gather at Wenceslas Square in Prague, Czechia, 03 November 2026, during a nationwide walkout by staff of public service broadcasters Czech Television and Czech Radio. Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA The UK government confirmed that two of the planes affected had departed from British airports.
The UK has one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we’ve seen today.
Our world-leading police and intelligence agencies work closely every day to keep us safe, using the tools they have to assess and respond to potential threats.
It’s also worth recalling some other similar incidents in the last few weeks.
On 18 October, an Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to ​Vienna diverted to Sofia ‌after a reported bomb ​threat while over Romania, Reuters said.
And yesterday, on 2 November, a WizzAir flight from London to Sofia was diverted to Budapest after a bomb threat ( 10:44 ).
Reuters is carrying a quick confirmation that the flight from Bergamo to Sofia in Bulgaria was operated by WizzAir, not Ryanair.
This has also been updated in the tally at the top of the page.
Bringing it all together, seven bomb threats have now been reported in total:
LOT Polish Airlines flight from London Heathrow, UK to Warsaw Okęcie, diverted to Warsaw Modlin, Poland ( 10:33 , 10:58 , 12:00 , 13:57 ).
SAS flight from Copenhagen, Denmark to Warsaw Okęcie ( 11:33 , 12:59 ).
Ryanair flight from Manchester, UK to Murcia, Spain ( 12:44 , 13:44 )
Ryanair flight from Lisbon, Portugal to Rome, Italy ( 15:02 )
WizzAir flight from Bergamo, Italy to Sofia, Bulgaria ( 15:41 )
Ryanair flight from Dublin, Ireland to Sofia, Bulgaria
There is also an update from Bulgaria, with the country’s transport ministry telling Reuters the bomb threats were actually made against two planes from Bergamo in Italy and Dublin in Ireland, and not from Israel as previously reported.
That brings the total to seven planes (that we know of).
Back to Berlin, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy also rejects Russia’s suggestion of a meeting in Moscow as “counterproductive.” He says what’s needed is serious talks, and not a gimmick.
He also insists that Russia has no advantage on the frontline at the moment.
Merz then adds that the 19 November meeting will decide further support for Ukraine in 2027 , and that concludes the press.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a press conference with the German chancellor in Berlin. Photograph: Filip Singer/EPA Meanwhile, two more false bomb threats were reported in Italy involving Ryanair flights from Lisbon and Dublin to Rome’s Fiumicino Airport, according to the Italian newspapers La Repubblica and Corriere della Sera.
The plane from Dublin was escorted by two Italian air force fighter jets, newspaper reported.
In both cases, routine checks were confirmed as negative, meaning no threat was identified, SkyTG24 said.
That brings the total of flights affected by false alarms today to at least six, up from four reported earlier (that we know of).
Asked about his expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks, Zelenskyy says he hopes to see future security guarantees for Ukraine to be covered, alongside a “prosperity package” that would help with the reconstruction of Ukraine.
He also says he hopes to discuss a proposal on energy, Black Sea truce, which is “in the interest of not only Ukraine, but also Russia and various nations in Africa.”
He reiterates that “there can be no stable peace unless Europe is at the negotiating table.”
Merz for his part says that “it is crucial for Russia to finally engage in serious negotiations.”
Responding, Zelenskyy thanks Germany for its continued help, including on air defence, and says that while many people will be following the events in the US today’s midterm elections, “the role of Europe – and specifically Germany – remains crucial.”
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends a press conference with German chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters He says he briefed Merz on the latest attacks on Ukraine .
He also confirms the upcoming Abu Dhabi talks on 10-11 November ( 11:21 ) , which he says hopefully “will pave the way for a trilateral meeting at the level of heads of states and government.”
He also confirms further talks on Ukraine will be held in Brussels on Wednesday ( 12:41 ), as per the European Commission’s announcement earlier, and that the coalition of the willing will meet in Berlin on 19 November.
Germany’s Merz begins by saying Zelenskyy’s visit comes “at a critical moment” as Russian attacks on Ukraine continued with “undiminished – indeed, increasing – severity and ruthlessness.”
German chancellor Friedrich Merz attends a joint press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, in Berlin, Germany. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters He says Ukraine “can continue to rely on Germany,” with more support from Berlin in the coming months, including on air defence, energy, and broader winter-related aid.
Merz also warns that the outcome of the war in Ukraine “will determine European security for a long time to come.”
He says Germany will be coordinating with France and the UK, and will host a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin later this month.
The German chancellor also talks of growing concerns about the broader effects of the continuing war, including a potential “global food crisis” triggered by Russia’s continued attacks on trading routes in the Black Sea.
He says the upcoming Abu Dhabi talks are “the right step forward,” and Europe hopes to play its part.
In the meantime, Berlin and partners will “increase the pressure on Moscow and continue to support Ukraine,” he says.

items.content:
Several planes have been evacuated and searched including this Ryanair flight in Spain, after a hoax bomb threat.
Several planes have been evacuated and searched including this Ryanair flight in Spain, after a hoax bomb threat.
Seven planes across Europe searched or diverted after ‘malicious hoax’ bomb threats
Unclear if series of incidents affecting two UK departures and several Ryanair services, among others, were connected
Seven planes across Europe have been searched or diverted after a series of bomb threats were made to passenger flights, prompting questions as to whether there was any coordination behind the warnings.
Two UK departures – one from Heathrow and one from Manchester – were among those threatened in what Downing Street called “malicious hoaxes”, though all planes landed safely and no explosives were found.
A UK Department for Transport source added that the low-level threats were “not credible” and that passengers should not be concerned, though the warnings disrupted flights and prompted investigations across the UK and Europe.
None of the incidents and subsequent searches threw up any evidence of terrorist activity, though authorities were responding to an unusual number of reported threats in one day.
One of Warsaw’s two main airports, Modlin, was briefly closed after receiving a diverted plane, and Polish officials confirmed that they had received bomb threats involving two flights coming into the capital.
Italian fighter jets escorted a Ryanair plane into Rome following a warning of a suspected threat on a flight coming from Dublin. The flight landed safely and nothing untoward was reported as being found.
There was little obvious pattern surrounding the incidents, which affected flights taking off from the UK, Ireland, Denmark, Portugal and Italy, and landing in Poland, Spain, Italy and Bulgaria . Four of the flights were operated by Ryanair, the others by Wizz Air, LOT and SAS.
Investigators added there was no immediate evidence of a hostile state being behind the threats, though they continued to monitor developments, sharing information across the continent while inquiries continued.
A police officer and sniffer dog inspect a Ryanair airplane in Spain. Photograph: Forta/Reuters Aviation security fears have been reignited with the recent FlyDubai incident when a co-pilot allegedly attempted to crash a Tel Aviv-bound plane. Russia has also been accused of being behind firebomb threats targeting parcel carriers using cargo planes over the past two years.
The threats followed an incident on Monday when another flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted, apparently without substance.
Experts said that fake threats occur on a daily basis. Philip Baum, visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University, said: “Most are from individuals who think it is funny or want to delay a flight for some reason. If the industry was to respond to every unsubstantiated threat, flights would grind to a halt.
“The reality is that terrorist organisations who might like to smuggle a bomb on to a flight don’t tell people, they claim responsibility after the attacks.”
But he added that the fact that some aircraft did divert would “imply that the threats are credible and specific in nature, and therefore one has to respond accordingly”.
Tuesday’s series of incidents started with a flight from Heathrow operated by the Polish carrier LOT, which was scheduled to arrive at Warsaw’s Chopin airport but was diverted to the second airport, further from the Polish capital, Modlin. Authorities closed that airport after the alert and the Boeing 737 Max landed without incident.
“The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found,” spokesperson Adam Szablowski told AFP. “The airport has been reopened and is operating normally.”
An SAS aircraft flying from Copenhagen lands at Warsaw Chopin airport in Poland after receiving a bomb threat. Photograph: Piotr Bozyk/Reuters A Scandinavian Airlines plane from Copenhagen to Warsaw was also the subject of a threat but landed at Chopin airport, where a security inspection that did not turn up any explosive devices closed part of the airport.
Another UK departure, a Ryanair plane from Manchester, was met by emergency vehicles on landing at its destination, Murcia in southern Spain , after another threat. Spanish regional authorities confirmed on social media that no explosives were found on the flight.
The Metropolitan police confirmed its aviation unit is monitoring the situation, adding no security issues were identified following threats made against flights after they had taken off.
A UK government spokesperson said of the threats to two departures from Britain: “The UK has one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we’ve seen today.
“Our world-leading police and intelligence agencies work closely every day to keep us safe, using the tools they have to assess and respond to potential threats.”
In Italy, two Ryanair flights were searched at Rome’s Fiumicino airport following potential bomb threats, according to the airport operator ADR. The first was a flight from Lisbon, while a second later in the morning from Dublin was escorted in by Italian air force fighter jets until landing.
A Wizz Air plane in Budapest on Monday night after being diverted because of a bomb threat on its way from London Luton to Sofia. Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty Images Bulgaria’s ​transport ‌ministry said ‌in a statement to ‌Reuters that threats were ​made against a Wizz Air flight ⁠from Bergamo and a Ryanair flight from Dublin to ⁠the capital, Sofia. Both flights were carrying about 180 passengers and landed safely, with no devices found.
The separate incidents came the day after a Wizz Air service from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet.
The plane, which was due to depart from Luton at 8.15am on Monday for Sofia, was diverted after a bomb threat was received “during the flight”, Wizz Air said.
Airlines abide by a regulated process to assess and manage bomb threats, although virtually all are fake. In the UK, airlines file a mandatory occurrence report to the Civil Aviation Authority .

items.title: Iran Says Four Oil Tankers Hit Naval Mines in Strait of Hormuz as Tensions With US Escalate - Kurdistan24
items.summary: Iran Says Four Oil Tankers Hit Naval Mines in Strait of Hormuz as Tensions With US Escalate  Kurdistan24
items.content:
Iran Says Four Oil Tankers Hit Naval Mines in Strait of Hormuz as Tensions With US Escalate
IRGC claims vessels attempting to cross without Tehran's authorization were destroyed, as Ghalibaf says Americans voted “NO TO WAR” following Democratic gains in the midterm elections
Iranians wave flags in front of an anti-US and anti-Israel billboard during a rally in Tehran's Enghelab Square, Nov. 3, 2026
ERBIL (Kurdistan24) — Four oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said Wednesday, raising fresh concerns over maritime security and global energy supplies amid renewed military tensions between Tehran and Washington.
"Four non-compliant oil tankers attempting to pass through the prohibited passage south of the Strait of Hormuz were destroyed after striking naval mines and are still burning," the IRGC said in a statement carried by Iranian state television.
The Guards added that two other vessels had been stopped and claimed that Iranian forces had shot down a drone over the strategic waterway. The statement did not identify the tankers, their owners, or the nationalities of their crews.
The announcement came a day after US President Donald Trump confirmed that American forces had carried out strikes against Iran, following reports of an attack on Qeshm Island, the largest island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump described the operation as a limited strike targeting an Iranian anti-aircraft installation, while playing down speculation that Washington was preparing a broader military campaign.
The latest developments threaten to further undermine an already fragile situation surrounding the strait, through which a substantial share of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas supplies normally passes.
Ghalibaf links US election results to opposition to war
Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the United States, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, on Wednesday interpreted the US midterm election results as a rejection of the war by American voters, following Democratic gains and Republican setbacks.
"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Ghalibaf posted on X.
His remarks came after Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections, which were held amid public dissatisfaction with the conflict and concerns over its economic consequences, including rising living costs.
Ghalibaf's comments added a political dimension to Tehran's response to Washington's latest military action, as Iranian officials continue to present the United States with a choice between diplomatic negotiations and renewed confrontation.
Since the conflict erupted in February with large-scale US and Israeli strikes against Iran, Tehran has sought to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, targeting vessels attempting to cross without its authorization.
The disruption has turned the narrow maritime corridor into one of the conflict's most consequential pressure points, with implications extending well beyond the region.
Any prolonged interruption to shipping could disrupt energy markets, increase transportation and insurance costs, and place additional pressure on countries dependent on Gulf energy exports.
The conflict has remained largely at a stalemate for months, despite continuing indirect contacts between Washington and Tehran through regional mediators.
Iran has indicated its willingness to reopen the waterway, but has conditioned such a move on Washington accepting a series of demands, including an end to the war, the unfreezing of Iranian assets, the lifting of oil sanctions, and an end to US restrictions on Iranian ports.
Ghalibaf struck a defiant tone earlier, saying the Islamic Republic was "ready for battle with its finger on the trigger."
However, President Masoud Pezeshkian maintained that his government was seeking to resolve the confrontation through diplomatic channels.
"No one will benefit from this war" if fighting resumes, Pezeshkian said on Tuesday, underscoring the competing messages emerging from Tehran as military tensions rise and negotiations remain uncertain.
With Washington and Tehran continuing to exchange warnings while maintaining indirect diplomatic contacts, the latest incidents in the Strait of Hormuz risk turning an already fragile confrontation into a wider threat to regional stability and international energy security.

items.title: Key moments from a night of midterm election firsts
items.summary: Democrats have taken control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency - proving moments of celebration.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
By Nardine Saad ,Â  Reporting from Los Angeles, California Â  and Â  James FitzGerald
Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Even before the full vote tallies are known, projected results have provided the party with a number of things to celebrate - and rival Republicans some reasons to commiserate. These are some of the key moments so far.
Jeffries talks of 'great American comeback' after historic results
Democrats have tallied up victories in states that were comfortably won by Trump two years ago, registering sizeable swings in the likes of Texas, Kansas, Ohio and South Carolina.
Among the senior party figures who have cheered the results are Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.
"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.
If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Johnson.
Anthony Zurcher: Democrats tear up Trump's political map on historic night
Trump congratulates opposition on 'good job'
Trump spoke throughout the evening to a number of US media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job".
He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Texas.
Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."
He acknowledged that the US-Israel war on Iran, which has impacted on consumer prices in the US, had affected the vote, saying: "Iran was a piece of it."
Susan Collins, who has served as the Republican senator for Maine for three decades, is one indicator of the scale of the Republican losses.
She was felled by Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, a logger who sought to point to his background to persuade blue-collar Mainers to vote for him.
In a statement reported by US media, Collins conceded defeat and said it had been the "honour of my life" to serve the state for 30 years.
Collins entered the race one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election, and found that her tactic to distance herself from Trump did not work.
The BBC's Helena Humphrey described a sombre atmosphere at Collins's watch party in the city of Maine - where the song Closing Time was played.
Republican Susan Collins loses seat to Democrat, ending nearly 30 years in the Senate
With James Talarico winning a seat in the US Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa being elected state governor, Democrats scored two statewide victories in Texas - ending a string of defeats they have endured for almost two generations.
Talarico's supporters went beserk as the projected results arrived at an election-night party, wrote the BBC's Gary O'Donoghue. Attendees hugged, kissed and drank to a reality they dared not believe would come true.
Hinojosa becomes the first Latina to be elected governor of the state.
Among the other states where history was made by the Democrats were Kansas, where Adam Hamilton took a closely-fought Senate seat - giving the state its first Democratic senator for nearly a century.
Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes first black female governor in US
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, has won the governor's race in Georgia, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.
The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue, which came after the state's former senator said the party was "nauseously optimistic" about their chances this year.
Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive. The state has also not had a Democratic governor in more than 20 years.
Image caption, Keisha Lance Bottoms beat billionaire businessman Rick Jackson
Elsewhere in the state, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won a second term in another closely-watched race.
The speculation surrounding Ossoff's plans for the next presidential election in 2028 will likely increase. He is considered a potential leading contender if he throws his hat in the ring, though he has denied having any such plan.
Figure caption, Democrat Jon Ossoff projected to hold key Georgia Senate seat
Chris Pappas celebrates with husband as first openly gay man elected to Senate
Figure caption, Watch: "I am ready to fight" - Senator-elect Chris Pappas celebrates New Hampshire win
Democrat Chris Pappas has also made history as the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.
Pappas defeated former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race, whom he thanked on Tuesday, saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."
The 46-year-old Pappas had represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019 but chose not to run for re-election so he could launch his campaign for the Senate.
Among the other firsts of the night were in Florida, where Republican Byron Donalds has become the state's first black governor, following a hearty endorsement from Trump.
The result was one of the few high points of an otherwise difficult evening for the Republicans.

Zelenskyy says 33 killed while more than 50 could be trapped in the rubble in Komyshuvakha; Russia hammers Ukraine’s ⁠energy infrastructure. What we know on day 1,715
Thirty-three people were killed and more than 50 could be trapped in rubble a day after multiple Russian strikes on a Ukrainian village , Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday, calling it one of Moscow’s worst attacks of the war. Rescue operations were ongoing in the frontline south-eastern village of Komyshuvakha, where Russian forces had struck a former school building that Ukraine said was being used to distribute aid. The attack hit after a ceasefire held for several days in the Kherson region, Pjotr Saeur reports , allowing for a rare humanitarian mission.
Russia bombarded Ukraine’s ⁠energy infrastructure in waves on Tuesday, knocking out power to swathes of the country with dozens of missiles and hundreds of drones, a week before US-brokered peace talks were due to resume . Zelenskyy said Russia had launched 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles overnight , hitting power plants and substations from the Black Sea port of Odesa in the south to Rivne in the west. Ukraine’s largest private generating company, DTEK, said three of its five thermal power plants had been knocked offline. The Kyiv ‌mayor, Vitali Klitschko, writing on Telegram, described the situation with power in the city as “extremely difficult”.
Emergency responders comb through rubble after deadly strike on Ukrainian aid centre – video
A further suspect has been arrested in connection with a fire at a Polish Starlink station in September , German prosecutors said Tuesday. The Turkish national was detained in the southern German city of Reutlingen, three weeks after two other Turkish suspects were also arrested in Germany over the same case. The two men arrested in October are in custody ahead of their possible extradition to Poland. Polish prime minister Donald Tusk has called the fire an “act of hybrid warfare”, at a time when Ukraine’s allies have accused Moscow of such hybrid attacks .
Ukraine has opened an investigation into reports a group of alleged army deserters had been held against their will , an incident that renewed focus on the sensitive issue of military conscription during Russia’s invasion. The State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) announced the probe after reports circulated on social media of “the allegedly illegal detention of soldiers” at a house in the Kyiv region, it said in a statement on Tuesday. Agence France-Presse reported videos circulating on social media showed angry crowds outside the house, where the SBI said clashes had erupted.
Management at Ukraine’s Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant ⁠said on Tuesday that a Ukrainian drone had killed two people ⁠in a car , ⁠including a ​female employee. The statement gave no indication where the ⁠incident occurred. It said the employee was the third killed in the past ⁠two weeks and the 13th since April. “Attacks on ​civilian cars, killing ‌of peaceful ‌people – this is targeted terrorism. People must not ‌become targets,” the statement said. Ukraine did not comment.
Norway, Denmark, Sweden and the Czech Republic will refuse to play Russia at the next year’s men’s Ice Hockey world champion ship in Germany due to safety concerns and ⁠geopolitical tensions, their national federations said ⁠Tuesday. The Court of ​Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled last week to allow Russia to compete in International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) events again, overturning the governing body’s decision to exclude Russian teams following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

items.title: NVIDIA Rises 3% Despite AI CEO's Warning on Chinese Chip Competition; AMD Climbs 5%, Broadcom Gains 3% - 24/7 Wall St.
items.summary: NVIDIA Rises 3% Despite AI CEO's Warning on Chinese Chip Competition; AMD Climbs 5%, Broadcom Gains 3%  <font color="#6f6f6
items.content:
NVIDIA Rises 3% Despite AI CEO's Warning on Chinese Chip Competition; AMD Climbs 5%, Broadcom Gains 3%
A startup CEO backed by NVIDIA just called Chinese open-source AI models a Trojan horse for Chinese chips, yet semiconductor investors shrugged off the warning and sent chip stocks higher anyway. Here is what explains the disconnect.
The Nvidia logo displayed on a smartphone screen, set against a backdrop of upward-trending green stock charts, visually represents the company's strong market performance highlighted in the article. © Shutterstock / Below the Sky
A warning that Chinese AI labs could soon sell chips abroad isn't keeping buyers away from NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ). NVIDIA stock traded at $208.24 in the afternoon, up 3% from Monday's close of $202.06. The gain snaps a four-session losing streak. Even so, NVIDIA stock remains down 11% over the past month.
This rebound has lifted NVIDIA's market value to $5.03 trillion. The Wall Street Journal reported that the chipmaker has reclaimed the title of world's most valuable company from Apple ( NASDAQ:AAPL ). Semiconductor stocks broadly are bouncing back from recent turbulence, with the U.S. midterm elections in focus.
Reflection AI CEO Flags Chinese Chips Riding Along With Open Models
Misha Laskin, CEO of NVIDIA-backed startup Reflection AI, warned in comments reported November 3 that Chinese AI labs giving away open models abroad will start selling their own hardware alongside them. Laskin called open models "Trojan horses for the infrastructure that they bring." Chinese companies selling open models into the Middle East, other Asian countries or Brazil "will now also start selling chips and their data centers," he said. That's a challenge aimed directly at NVIDIA's ecosystem.
NVIDIA has already removed China from its forecasts . Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress said on the company's August 26 earnings call, "Given ongoing geopolitical uncertainty, there is no China data center compute revenue in our forward outlook." China revenue, including Hong Kong, fell to $19.7 billion in fiscal 2026 from $25.0 billion the prior year. What Laskin describes hits a different pool: NVIDIA's sales outside both the U.S. and China, where sovereign AI revenue grew 35% sequentially in Q2 FY2027.
Another China-related development for NVIDIA emerged the same day. The Financial Times reported on November 3 that NVIDIA has told its cloud clients to sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies.
The valuation helps explain why buyers shrugged off both items. At 17x forward earnings, NVIDIA trades at a five-year low, versus a five-year average of 36x. Supply is the other buffer, with CEO Jensen Huang telling analysts in August, "Even though our demand is much greater than 70%, our supply allows us to confidently deliver 70%." Such a gap suggests Chinese hardware competition may weigh more on NVIDIA's growth beyond fiscal 2028 than on near-term sales.
Advanced Micro Devices ( NASDAQ:AMD ) stock is at $491.87, up 5%, the strongest gain among the three. Q3 2026 results from AMD arrive after the close on November 3, offering a near-term read on AI chip demand ahead of NVIDIA's own report.
Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) stock is at $332.63, up 3%, running a step ahead of NVIDIA. With all three chip names rising together, NVIDIA's move looks like part of a sector-wide recovery.
How NVIDIA's Platform Model Differs From AMD and Broadcom
NVIDIA sells graphics processing units (GPUs), central processing units (CPUs), networking gear and software as one platform that runs in every major cloud. Huang framed it on the August call: "NVIDIA is a platform, an entire AI factory platform that spans the entire AI life cycle, that you can use in any cloud." AMD competes as a merchant alternative for GPUs and server CPUs, while Broadcom builds custom accelerators and networking chips designed around individual hyperscalers' needs.
That breadth shapes how NVIDIA meets the threat Laskin described. On the same call, Huang said, "Nearly all open models run on NVIDIA, and the reason for that is because NVIDIA's footprint around the world is the highest, and our architecture is the most fungible." Chinese labs matching their own chips with open models would be competing for that same global footprint.
Chinese Competition Raises Pressure on the Next NVIDIA Report
NVIDIA has scheduled its Q3 FY2027 results for November 17, and the company guided for revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. The next test for NVIDIA is whether management describes demand outside the U.S. and China as holding firm against bundled Chinese offerings.
The bull case rests on a forward multiple at a five-year low and NVIDIA's demand that still exceeds supply. The bears see a risk that Chinese models, chips and data centers sold as a package could erode NVIDIA's position in the Middle East, Asia and Latin America over time. A cautious approach could make sense while the Chinese hardware threat abroad plays out, and the picks-and-shovels names driving the global AI expansion, from grid equipment to cooling, are worth a look too (we covered seven of them in a free report on AI infrastructure suppliers that aren't chipmakers ).

items.title: Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash
items.summary: At least 69 people were killed and dozens injured in the collision south of the capital, Madrid.
items.content:
Image caption, Ãscar Puente had been under mounting pressure as opposition parties and some allies of the government called on him to step down
By Guy Hedgecoe ,Â  Madrid Â  and Â  Jaroslav Lukiv
Spain's Transport Minister Ãscar Puente has resigned - six days after the high-speed train collision in which at least 69 people were killed and dozens injured.
He announced his decision in Congress, after giving evidence on last Wednesday's disaster near the town of Urda, south of the capital Madrid, in which a train smashed into the back of a stationary train.
"A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year," he said - a reference to January's crash on the same line which left 46 people dead.
Last week's crash was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Image caption, Rescuers had to use heavy lifting equipment to get access to derailed carriages where a number of passengers were trapped
Puente announced his decision at the end of a lengthy congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and had been grilled by the opposition.
He also said: "I am not only stepping down from my position as minister of transport, but... I am also withdrawing my name from the lists for the early legislative elections."
Puente's position immediately came under scrutiny after the 28 October crash.
The main opposition, the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox, were both calling for his resignation - as were some of the government's allies.
They argued that the minister should take responsibility for a high-speed rail system that many Spaniards now regard as unsafe and whose credibility even Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez admitted was "broken".
The opposition also criticised Puente for appearing to blame human error for the crash, claiming the minister was trying to deflect the blame from his own failings.
But, having said he was going to remain in his post just a few days ago, his resignation appears to have taken many by surprise.
The rail accident and Puente's decision have come at a crucial moment in the Spanish political calendar, with early general elections on 29 November.
Many observers see the accident as a massive electoral setback to the Socialist-led government that will make it impossible for SÃ¡nchez to defy the polls and win the election.
Puente's predicament presented him and the prime minister with a dilemma - refusing to resign might look insensitive in the wake of the accident and stepping down could look like acknowledging he and the government were at fault.
In the end, Puente opted for the second option, insisting his decision had been driven by "political dignity".
The prime minister praised his colleague who had "faced up to the situation, provided answers and solutions, and then stepped aside".
"Out of dignity. Of his own accord. Out of respect for the victims," SÃ¡nchez added.
Many Spaniards will now ask whether Puente's successors will manage to restore faith in the country's railway system.
Last Wednesday's accident involved a train run by state-owned operator Renfe with 397 passengers on board and a stationary train run by private operator Iryo, which was carrying 147 passengers.
A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media soon after the crash revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the disaster.
The three recordings of conversations between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that the Renfe train was given clearance to move even though the other train had stopped on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Figure caption, Listen: Audio recordings between train driver and controller
In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties.
After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."
The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."
The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.
The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.
The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.

Prime minister Mark Carney says no Russian or Belarusian ice hockey athletes will be competing for their countries in Canada. Photograph: Matias Delacroix/AP
Canada joins coalition refusing to play ice hockey against Russia over Ukraine war
Growing number of countries are resisting Russia’s reintegration into international hockey after a sports court lifted a ban on competition
Canada has joined a coalition of countries refusing to play ⁠ice ​hockey teams from Russia, with prime minister Mark Carney saying Russian skaters will not be able to compete in ⁠a world junior championship next month due to the war in Ukraine .
“While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific ‌war in Ukraine, as long as that’s going on, there will be none of ​those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” Carney told reporters on Tuesday.
Carney’s comments follow announcements by a growing number of national hockey federations that they will not play Russian teams, after ‌a decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to allow ‌Russians to compete in International Ice Hockey Federation (IHF) events.
An IIHF ban on Russian teams took ⁠effect after Moscow began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has been extended ​annually.
After several appeals by Russia’s hockey ‌federation, the CAS finally ‌lifted the ban on Friday, contending safety and security worries “were not supported by sufficient evidence”.
Russia bombs humanitarian hub in Ukraine, killing at least 31 people
On Monday, the Finnish Ice Hockey Association asked other nations to stand up against the decision. Federations representing Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Latvia and the Czech Republic announced Tuesday they sided with Finland.
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday thanked European nations for “refusing to share the ice with Russia”.
“If CAS lacks a moral compass, let’s show that hockey still has values,” he said in a post on X. “Refuse to play against Russia and deny visas to its players. Keep Russia off the ice! A war of aggression and hockey are incompatible.”
The Norwegians ‌were the first to announce on Tuesday their intention to play games in tournaments against all teams but those involving Russia.
“Our position that Russia should be excluded from all international championships as long as the war in Ukraine continues … remains unchanged,” Norway’s federation posted to social media.
“At this time, this decision is based on our responsibility to ‌protect the safety and wellbeing of our players, team staff and their families. We believe playing against Russia under the current circumstances could expose our players ​and team staff to significant security risks.”
Similar statements followed from the other three nations.
The CAS ruling has left cities worldwide to decide whether they will host upcoming tournaments, as planned, should Russians compete as the war continues in Ukraine.
The world junior ​tournament is scheduled to ​begin 26 December in Alberta.

Motorcyclists drive past a billboard depicting a Persian legendary hero and flying figure hitting U.S. aircraft carriers alongside the message: "From the Persian Gulf a new power rises" "The army of Satan will be drowned in the Persian Gulf," in Tehran, Iran, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 US hits Qeshm Island, Pezeshkian signals more diplomacy: Iran war latest
list 2 of 4 Iran’s anti-negotiation hardliners turn against President Pezeshkian
list 4 of 4 Mediators continue US-Iran negotiations amid war rhetoric: What we know
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei , the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process “.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack .
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while attempting to pass through a prohibited shipping lane south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The tankers remained ablaze following the explosions, the IRGC said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency. Two other vessels were detained for violating shipping restrictions, it added.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
It could not be independently verified whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and the IRGC were linked.
The IRGC also claimed its air defence forces shot down a US-made MQ-9 drone over the strait at 4.30am local time (01:00GMT), describing it as the 56th such aircraft it had downed.
The statement said the operations were carried out by the IRGC’s naval and aerospace forces, which had inflicted “heavy blows on the enemy”.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

Midterm Democrat Gains Likely To Put Trump's Russia, Ukraine, Iran Policies Under Pressure
Midterm Democrat Gains Likely To Put Trump's Russia, Ukraine, Iran Policies Under Pressure
Midterm elections in the United States on November 3 saw the Democratic Party take control of Congress.
WASHINGTON -- Democratic Party victories in the US midterm elections are set to shift the balance of power in Congress, giving the party greater oversight and influence over legislation, with implications for US policy toward Russia, Ukraine, and Iran.
A wave of Democrat victories at voting booths across the country on November 3 is projected to wrest control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives from President Donald Trump's Republicans, according to projections by several major US news organizations.
The results represent a significant shift in congressional power, giving Democrats greater influence over federal spending, administration oversight, and presidential nominations.
US Strikes Iranian Island As Trump Downplays Prospect Of Renewed Conflict
Trump said he was willing to accept the election results and work with Democrats, according to The New York Times. "We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," Trump was quoted as saying.
Trump retains broad authority over diplomacy and military operations, while Republican opposition and the president's veto power could limit efforts to translate Democratic victories into legislative changes.
The election comes as the United States and Israel remain at war with Iran, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues, and Washington's approach to Moscow remains a source of bipartisan disagreement.
The most immediate foreign policy test for the incoming Congress may be the war with Iran.
Democrats campaigned on ending the conflict, which has contributed to rising energy prices and economic uncertainty. Their control of both chambers will strengthen their ability to scrutinize the administration, challenge military spending, and push for limits on military operations.
Dania Arayssi, program head and senior analyst at the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, who regularly briefs congressional and executive branch decision-makers, told RFE/RL that the election results could push Trump toward a diplomatic exit from the war.
"The outcomes of the election, particularly seeing the Democrats winning the House and the Senate, will definitely push the Trump administration to push for an exit strategy from the war, particularly through diplomatic tools and negotiations," she said.
Arayssi said Democrats could block additional funding for the conflict and investigate the administration's decisions once the new Congress convenes in January.
Sanctions, War, Isolation: Why Hasn't Iran's Hard-Line Government Collapsed?
She argued Tehran could also seek better terms in negotiations, calculating that Trump's political ability to sustain the military campaign has weakened.
"This also means that the Iranians will not be under pressure to offer any additional compromise," she said.
Many analysts also cautioned that despite the Democrats' landslide victory, the impact is far from predetermined.
Trump remains commander-in-chief and retains considerable authority over military operations and diplomacy. Most Republicans have defended the Iran campaign as necessary to counter Iranian nuclear and regional threats and are likely to resist Democratic efforts to restrict funding.
Nevertheless, the economic consequences of the conflict have become a political liability for the administration. Higher gasoline and diesel prices, partly linked to disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats make affordability a central campaign issue.
The incoming Congress could also intensify scrutiny of the Pentagon and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, while funding negotiations could create further confrontations with the White House.
US, Russia, Ukraine To Resume Peace Talks Amid Doubts Over Breakthrough
Meanwhile for Kyiv, which has relied on US support for more than four years in its battle to repel invading Russian forces, the results bring both uncertainty and reassurance.
Several prominent congressional supporters of Ukraine are leaving office, including Republican Representative Don Bacon, a vocal critic of Russia who has frequently broken with his party and the White House over support for Kyiv.
"I'm an old-school Reagan Republican and see the Russian invasion of Ukraine [as] the most important crisis facing the free world," Bacon told RFE/RL on November 3.
"I hope we elect a 120th Congress that is stronger in its support for our friend and ally," he added.
However, other departing Republican lawmakers include former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, Senators Thom Tillis, Bill Cassidy, and John Cornyn, as well as Representative Michael McCaul. Their departures remove several influential voices who have advocated a tougher approach toward Moscow.
Nevertheless, Ukrainian-American organizations say they believe support for Kyiv will remain bipartisan.
"While we are losing titan supporters of Ukraine in this election cycle, we are mindful of those who will remain and are encouraged on a bipartisan manner that Ukraine will still garner significant support," Michael Sawkiw, president of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, told RFE/RL.
Sawkiw identified congressional oversight of the administration's recent waiver of Russia sanctions and its diesel deal, increased security assistance to Ukraine, and an extension of Temporary Protected Status for Ukrainian refugees as priorities.

items.content:
Democrats win control of Congress; experts say little will change for Ukraine, Europe
Democrats took control of Congress in the 2026 U.S. midterms, but Donald Trump will retain broad powers over foreign policy, limiting changes to U.S. support for Ukraine and relations with the European Union.
Supporters cheer for U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas (John Anderson/Alamy Live News)
A blue wave rolled across the United States last night.
With results still filtering in, Democrats looked poised to win both chambers of the U.S. Congress — the Senate and the House — decisively.
It represents a sizable victory for the Democratic Party, but analysts don't expect the shift in political winds to significantly alter Donald Trump's foreign policy toward Ukraine and the rest of Europe.
Due to the relatively weak foreign policy powers of Congress and Trump's embrace of executive power, even a Democratic-controlled Congress can only play a marginal role in shifting Trump's approach.
Until America's 2028 presidential election, Trump will continue to call the shots, such as by putting additional pressure on Ukraine to take a peace deal with Russia, and the possible use of new tariffs powers against the European Union.
"The Trump administration's foreign policy is like a car going down the highway," said James Green, a research fellow at the Center for European Reform and former Congressional aide in Washington. "Congress has the ability to slow that car down, maybe make it put on a turn signal, but it's going to be very difficult for Congress to change the overall route over the next two years."
With control of both chambers, the Democratic Party now holds Congress' constitutionally granted foreign policy powers, such as declaring war, appropriating funds for the military, confirming nominations, regulating foreign commerce and overseeing the executive branch.
However, since the Vietnam War, Congress has handed over a large number of its foreign policy powers to the executive, according to Nevada Joan Lee, a policy fellow with the European Council on Foreign Relations.
"You see consistently when something arises, Congress deferring to the presidency to make a foreign policy decision," she said.
Congress still has some tools to shape American foreign policy, but they've been blunted in recent years.
For example, Congress controls key legislative files that must pass each year for the government to function — such as the National Defense Authorization Act that sets troop levels in Europe or reconciliation bills to fund the government. However, Trump has repeatedly refused to use the spending authorized by Congress, a process called pocket recissions, according to Joan Lee.
That means if the Congress wanted to restore funding to Ukraine, Trump may simply choose to not spend the money, she said.
Another tool at Congress' disposal is threatening a government shutdown over spending bills. However, because foreign policy carries little weight in American domestic politics, it's unlikely Democrats would risk a shutdown to restore funding to Ukraine, for example. A shutdown is far more likely over an issue like healthcare.
Congress also holds oversight authority over the executive branch and could summon members of Trump's foreign policy team for hearings. However, Trump has claimed executive privilege on a widening array of his decision-making powers, making it more difficult for Congress to call in members of his administration.
"I don't think the midterms will dramatically shape Trump's policy toward Europe one way or another," said Peter Rough, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, a conservative think tank in Washington D.C.
Juraj Majcin, a policy analyst at the European Policy Centre, said that a poor showing by the Republicans could "frustrate" Trump and "prompt him to double down on efforts to restrict U.S. support for Ukraine."
In fact, in some key areas of foreign policy Congress may have handed the Trump administration additional tools that could lead to more pressure on Ukraine and Europe.
In September, Congress passed the Graham Act to impose significant sanctions on Russia and countries buying Russian oil. But last month, Trump deferred the sanctions on Russia in exchange for a diesel deal with Putin.
The legislation also grants the White House additional tariff power, including against countries that continue to import Russian oil — potentially giving Trump a potent, legally sound weapon against European countries still buying Russian fuel, according to Joan Lee.
"This pretty much opens up any EU country to attack from the president on these tariffs," she said. "It took a lot of power out of Congress's hands."
MEP Bernd Lange (S&D, DE) said that a Democratic victory "could lead to more confrontational decisions, especially on trade and tariffs" from Trump. "A lame duck could become an angry duck," he added.
The next big shift in U.S. foreign policy toward Europe and Ukraine won't come until 2028, when the next American presidential elections will be held, according to Green.
Members states and the EU need to start engaging now with incoming members of Congress and 2028 presidential candidates on both the Democratic and Republican side, to begin shaping how those candidates view Europe — and what the transatlantic relationship could look like post-Trump, said Green and Joan Lee.
The progressive left-wing of the Democratic Party should be of special concern, according to Joan Lee. She said that conversations with progressive aides in the Democratic Party revealed an eagerness to anchor a possible transatlantic relationship under a more progressive administration in industrial policy, tech regulation and climate change — rather than on security.
That could mean a possible progressive president would hesitate to increase troop levels in Europe, according to Joan Lee.
However, for all the importance the U.S. plays in the EU and Ukraine, the continent's troubles have remained relatively marginal in U.S. politics.
"The biggest risk that Europeans risk with the Democratic Party is falling into some sort of irrelevance," said Joan Lee.

items.title: Seven flights across Europe targeted by suspected bomb threats
items.summary: Planes in Poland, Spain, Bulgaria and Italy have been checked for explosives following separate threats.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Sniffer dog inspects Ryanair plane in Spain after suspected bomb threat
By Emer Moreau ,Â  Jaroslav Lukiv Â  and Â  Laura Gozzi ,Â  Europe reporter
Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.
Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.
The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until landing. Authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria.
While officially there is no link between them, authorities from various countries will be co-operating to assess whether this was a co-ordinated attack, designed to disrupt airspace.
The UK government described the incidents as "malicious hoax threats".
In a statement it said it had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today".
Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".
"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".
A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.
Image caption, Two of the four flights were en route to Warsaw Chopin airport
In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.
Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.
One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.
One passenger later said she was unaware of the bomb threat until after the plane landed.
"We weren't told anything during the flight," Sarah told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The plane stopped quite suddenly and then we were kept on the runway for around 30 minutes."
"Then the fire engines turned up, the bomb squad turned up and we were asked to evacuate," she continues.
Sarah said the plane had not been on the ground a minute before it was "surrounded by fire engines and police and a bomb squad". All the passengers were then escorted by police, leaving all their belongings.
"We were only later told that it was an actual threat, a bomb threat to the plane itself," she added.
Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.
The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.
A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.
Later on Tuesday, Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said there were bomb threats against two planes travelling to the country's capital Sofia.
He told the state-owned Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) the flights were from the northern Italian city of Bergamo and Ireland's capital Dublin.
The flights into Sofia were not diverted and no explosives were found when the planes were checked, Peev said.
Bulgaria's border police said in a statement sent to the BBC that at around 10:35 (08:35 GMT) it had received an email about "the presence of an improvised explosive device on a flight returning from Bergamo".
"Standard procedures for such incidents were immediately activated, and an operational headquarters comprising representatives of various institutions was convened," the statement said.
The border police added that the same email also reported a "similar threat against aircraft arriving from Dublin".
Image caption, Initial checks found no explosives on board the Crown Iris cruise ship
In a separate development, a bomb alert triggered the evacuation of 1,537 passengers and crew from an Israel-bound cruise ship in Greece, media reports from both countries say.
Initial checks of the Panama-flagged Crown Iris vessel currently docked at a port on the Aegean island of Syros found no explosives, they said citing the Greek Coast Guard, and the ship was due to resume its journey.
Tuesday's aircraft incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.
Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.
BBC Verify has consulted aviation safety experts about what happens on board a plane when a bomb threat is issued.
Marco Chan, a former pilot for Cathay Pacific Airways and Hong Kong Airlines who is now a senior lecturer in aviation operations at Kingston University, said a bomb threat is considered "genuine until it is resolved, even though most turn out to be hoaxes".
Chan said crews will "quietly search" toilets, galleys and storage areas and will not touch a suspicious item unless it has to be taken to an area on the aircraft designated as the least risky bomb location.
The aircraft's captain will have multiple factors to assess, according to former airline pilot Terry Tozer, an aviation safety commentator.
He said these include what facilities are available at the airport they are being diverted to and how the plane can continue onwards should it turn out to be a false threat.
Chan added that once on the ground, the plane is generally "taken to an isolated stand, passengers are disembarked, and police and bomb disposal teams search it".
