items.content:
The year is 2006 . Democrats have swept the midterm congressional elections after a Republican administration launched an unpopular war in a Middle Eastern country. But the opposition pulls its punches and is unable to assert Congress' check on the president. The year is 2026. Democrats have swept the midterm congressional elections after a Republican administration launched an unpopular war in a Middle Eastern country. What will happen next?
Despite President Donald Trump's insistence that his "excursion" to Iran would be nothing like the invasion of Iraq, the domestic politics are looking quite similar. Both the failures of the war itself and the economic damage caused by setting an oil-rich region on fire became major political liabilities for the president's party. Exit polling shows that 62 percent of voters consider the war a mistake and 74 percent considered it a major factor in their votes. Some of the newly elected Democrats were upstarts who had ridden the wave of antiwar sentiment in the primaries to beat establishment favorites seen as complicit with the war.
"If it is still around next term, on day one, Democrats will pass a bill to end the Iran war," Rep. Ted Lieu (D–Calif.) told The New Republic in July 2026.
Translating that popular mandate into policy is easier said than done. Trump has shown multiple times that the president can simply veto or ignore war powers resolutions from Congress demanding an end to the war. Congress' only direct leverage is over the military budget—and threatening to withhold it is itself a politically risky maneuver, as newly elected lawmakers discovered after the 2006 elections. Party leadership that is willing to attack Republicans' execution of the war may not share a principled antiwar commitment.
"I had serious misgivings about the decision of this administration to go forward and still do. But it comes down to this. We have to decide whether or not we will provide the funds necessary to support the men and women in uniform…I don't support a precipitous withdrawal," Sen. Dick Durbin (D–Ill.) told NPR in May 2006, a few months before the midterms. He is still the Senate Democratic whip today.
Of course, there are important differences between now and then. The Iraq War was popular from the beginning and took some time to become unpopular, while the Iran war is the first U.S. war to start without majority support since mass opinion polling began. Rather than building legal support with an authorization from Congress, as President George W. Bush did for the Iraq War, the Trump administration simply attacked Iran by surprise and dared Congress to stop it.
The administration also stated from the beginning that it entered the war "at the request of and in the collective self-defense of its Israeli ally," tying the decision to a foreign nation that is becoming controversial in American politics. And unlike in Iraq, where U.S. troops quickly occupied the country and then became bogged down fighting guerrillas, the U.S. military is engaged in an on-again, off-again naval and aerial standoff with an intact Iranian government.
Still, the same tools that were available to Congress then are available to Congress now. "I would stop the funding. The House and the Senate should stop the funding for any further actions in the Iran war. That's what we did to stop the Vietnam War," Rep. Ro Khanna (D–Calif.) told Fox News the week before the midterm. (After a 1973 ceasefire in Vietnam, lawmakers forbade the Nixon administration from using any military funds to reenter the war.)
On paper, Khanna's faction can win this fight. Even some Republicans were shocked at the Trump administration's initial $200 billion funding request for the Iran war in March 2026. The administration folded the cost of the war into the general military budget a few months later, and all but six Democrats voted against that bill in the House of Representatives. Democrats now have at least a seven -seat House majority, which is expected to grow, according to AP News as of early Wednesday morning.
But they don't have the two-thirds majority necessary to override a presidential veto—and past experience shows that can be fatal for any attempt to defund the war. In 2007, the Bush administration asked the newly elected Congress for $93.4 billion to sustain U.S. forces in Iraq. Democrats initially passed a $123 billion bill  that gave the military until September 2008 to withdraw from the country. Bush vetoed it, claiming that the "terrorists" would simply "mark their calendars and gather their strength." Faced with a dilemma between giving Bush a blank check or leaving the military without funding, Democrats backed down, passing a war budget without a deadline. U.S. troops would stay for the entirety of the Bush administration.
The sporadic nature of the fighting with Iran does make the politics different from an ongoing ground war. Aside from U.S. naval escorts for oil tankers, which cost $2 billion to $3 billion per month, U.S. forces exclusively see action when there's a flare-up, which has only happened when Trump decided to escalate. "The only sure way to protect our troops is to end this war as soon as possible," Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer (D–N.Y.) contended .
The role of Israel is a double-edged sword for antiwar forces. On one hand, opponents of the Iran war can more easily deflect from accusations of unpatriotism and even present themselves as defending Americans' interests against foreigners. Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed argued that both Iran and Israel "have proven dangerous in their own way" during the Michigan debate . "Let's be honest about what happened here. Israel has pushed us to go to war in Iran," he said. "Ask yourself, are we safer because of that war?" El Sayed won the election and is now headed to the Senate.
On the other hand, the Trump administration can also claim that any decision to escalate the war again was out of its hands. Politico reported before the war began that some members of the Trump administration were hoping Israel would throw the first punch and invite Iranian retaliation. "We knew that there was going to be an Israeli action. We knew that that would precipitate an attack against American forces, and we knew that if we didn't preemptively go after them before they launched those attacks, we would suffer higher casualties," Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed a few days after the war began.
Weaker than restricting the budget but stronger than passing more war powers resolutions, Congress can use its investigative powers to squeeze the administration. So far, Democrats have demanded answers about U.S. troop casualties , U.S. attacks on civilians , the financial cost of the war, and even the role of " extreme religious beliefs " in military briefings. With a congressional majority, they can turn strongly worded letters into subpoenas for documents and witnesses with real legal weight.
And those investigations can turn into impeachments. "One of the first things we're going to do in the majority, we're going to run [Secretary of War] Pete Hegseth out of town," House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries (D–N.Y.) said last month, and The Telegraph reports that Democrats have already contacted whistleblowers willing to testify against him. Even before the new Congress takes office, the outgoing libertarian-leaning Rep. Thomas Massie (R–Ky.) has vowed to force a vote on Hegseth's impeachment.
Ultimately, the next Congress' role in the war comes down to Democrats' willingness to fight. The week before the war began, Democratic leadership delayed a vote on a war powers resolution. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D–Mich.) told Reason Editor Matt Welch on The Fifth Column that there was an "under-the-surface attempt to be like let's not do it, or let's not do it in a strong way" because lawmakers "fear the political consequences." Drop Site , meanwhile, reported that "many Democrats remain convinced a war with Iran is both the right policy and beneficial politically for them," because it would force Trump to own the cost of the conflict.
In June 2025, just before Israel launched the earlier Twelve Day War on Iran, Schumer mocked "TACO Trump," an acronym for "Trump Always Chickens Out," for "already folding" against "the terrorist government of Iran" in peace negotiations. On February 28, 2026, the day that Trump launched his current war, House leader Jeffries issued a waffling statement , agreeing that "Iran is a bad actor and must be aggressively confronted" but warning Trump not to make the war "costly" or "prolonged."
In fact, at one point, Democratic leadership threatened to become a bigger obstacle to ending the war than they were to starting it. When Trump signed a peace memorandum with Iran in June 2026, some Democrats attacked him as a weak appeaser. "This is not the art of the deal. This is the art of surrender," Schumer said on the Capitol steps, falsely claiming that the memorandum involved giving American taxpayer money to Iran and threatening to withhold any funding for it. The deal fell apart in July 2026.
The midterms have been a decisive rebuke to those politics. El Sayed, for example, won both the primary and the general election by calling his opponents complicit in the war—and dishonest in their opposition. "Now [Republican candidate] Mike Rogers wants you to believe that somehow he was not 100 percent aligned with Donald Trump on the war in the first place," El Sayed said at a September rally . "Here's the thing about war, you can't unring that bell."
Yet the post-2006 experience shows that talk is cheap, even talk about how the other guy isn't as serious. "The president may be content with keeping our troops mired in the middle of an open-ended civil war, but we're not, and neither are most Americans," the late Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D–Nev.) said in May 2007, two months before voting to let Bush keep U.S. troops mired in the middle of an open-ended civil war.

items.content:
By Henry Tugendhat , a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
An Iranian and a Chinese diplomat shakes hands in front of the flags of their countries.
Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zari (left) meets with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi at the Diaoyutai State Guesthouse in Beijing on May 13, 2018. Thomas Peter/AFP via Getty Images
In the 48 hours that followed the Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s main international airport, China’s major media outlets largely focused on an Iranian offer to help mediate between the two warring parties. The offer was made during a phone call between the Iranian and Saudi foreign ministers on Oct. 11, just hours after Houthi missiles killed 13 people and injured dozens more.
China’s enthusiastic coverage of Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi’s proposal comes on the back of an earlier report in September that China was privately pushing Iran to help mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. But it also speaks to why Beijing has little interest in pressuring Iran to end the war on Washington’s terms.

The offer was made during a phone call between the Iranian and Saudi foreign ministers on Oct. 11, just hours after Houthi missiles killed 13 people and injured dozens more.
China’s enthusiastic coverage of Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi’s proposal comes on the back of an earlier report in September that China was privately pushing Iran to help mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. But it also speaks to why Beijing has little interest in pressuring Iran to end the war on Washington’s terms.
China supports the Middle East taking greater responsibility for its own security, and its desire to see a reduced U.S. role in the region has long been a shared goal in the Sino-Iranian relationship.
For instance, in one 1981 study , Chinese scholars recommended that Beijing actively strengthen Iran’s position in the Gulf to hobble U.S. access to the region’s oil while seeking a carve-out for Chinese oil interests. And throughout the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq War, senior Chinese officials regularly called for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the Gulf and subsequently protested the U.S. intervention on Kuwait’s behalf when Iraq invaded the country in 1990.
More recently, China has toned down its calls for U.S. withdrawals from the region, but it still advocates for countries and regions to take responsibility for their own security interests in the multipolar world that China calls for. China’s Global Security Initiative is its most concrete expression of these interests.
Some might argue that Beijing’s significant economic interests in the region have made it beholden to U.S. security guarantees in recent years. It’s also true that China has always had a complicated relationship with Iran, often at arm’s length, and it seems unlikely that China would ever go to war on Iran’s behalf.
Perhaps this is why the Trump administration has so far misread Chinese interests. Perhaps most strikingly, U.S. President Donald Trump called on China to send ships to the Persian Gulf in March to assist in protecting commercial shipping lanes. China did not heed that call, but U.S. President Donald Trump may not have known that China was also the only permanent member of the U.N. Security Council not to send ships to protect sea-lanes during the Iran-Iraq War. This was despite the fact that China had joined the unanimous Security Council vote on Resolution 552 calling on Iran to cease attacks on neutral commerce in the Gulf. In other words, at a time when it was more critical of Iran’s conduct in war it still sought ways to avoid alienating Iran.
Yet it’s perfectly possible for China’s long-term goals and short-term conveniences to be true simultaneously. On the one hand, Beijing can advocate for a long-term shift toward regional self-reliance. On the other, it recognizes the advantages of U.S. security infrastructure for now.
Furthermore, China has often found its relationship with Iran to be very useful in dealing with the United States. For example, after Washington imposed arms embargoes over the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, China publicly acknowledged its nuclear cooperation programs with the Iranian government for the first time. Then, when Chinese leader Jiang Zemin and U.S. President Bill Clinton improved relations in the run-up to China’s accession to the World Trade Organization, Beijing agreed to cease nuclear cooperation with Iran in 1997 as a gesture of goodwill.
More cynically, one might take away from these examples that China’s willingness to pressure Iran has also depended on the U.S. ability to pressure China, but right now, it’s clear that Washington lacks both the leverage and the desire to pressure Beijing over Iran.
And so, China has no real incentive to lean on Iran to accept U.S. terms to end the war. Indeed, as soon as the headlines on Araghchi’s offer of support to Saudi Arabia subsided, Chinese media switched its focus back to Iran’s upper hand in negotiations with the United States, with headlines such as “Iran Says It Is Reviewing U.S. Proposals; Conditions for Reopening the Strait Remain Unchanged” and “Iran Claims a Significant Withdrawal of U.S. Naval Forces.”
China has also proved itself to be remarkably resilient in the face of lost oil imports. Lu Ruquan, a senior economist at China National Petroleum Corp., has argued that part of this stems from China’s success in developing 225 new oil and gas fields domestically between 2021 and 2025. But China also relies far less on oil than many countries. Where petroleum consists of 38 percent of total primary energy consumption in the United States , in China it’s closer to 18 percent.
Coal, meanwhile, still constitutes roughly 51 percent of China’s energy consumption and remains the bedrock of the country’s energy security. More than 90 percent of the coal China consumes is produced domestically, and over the past few years, the country’s domestically mined coal stocks have actually risen even as usage has dropped. China’s innovations and increasing use of renewable energy technologies have also played a significant role.
The Chinese economy can still be shaken by indirect effects of the oil crisis on pricing. But in the months leading up to the Iran war, China was struggling with deflation , not inflation. Increased price pressure therefore gives Beijing some relief from deflationary pressures, even if that scenario isn’t ideal.
Thus, it seems China’s greater diplomatic priority is mediating between Iran and the Gulf states for two main reasons. Firstly, it can help build China’s (and Iran’s) long-term interest in seeing a more regionally driven security architecture that relies less on the United States. But secondly, Beijing will be hoping that better relations between Iran and Gulf states may indirectly help improve China’s image among the Gulf countries that have grown frustrated by Beijing’s enabling of Iran’s war capabilities.
China’s leaders are likely not naive that this will happen soon or even involve Chinese weapons sales in the near term. Chinese scholar Niu Xinchun for one has observed that while Gulf states have started by buying weapons from more varied sources, those sources have so far not included China.
Nevertheless, as Trump prepares for the next round of meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping in November, he should be mindful of the long-term interests that China is also seeking to advance in the Middle East. More to the point, Trump should expect little help from Xi in getting out of his quagmire in Iran.
Henry Tugendhat is a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and research associate at the China-Africa Research Initiative at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies.

Hi there! My name is Janko Roettgers, and this is Lowpass. In this issue: Roku’s latest earnings show how the RAM shortage impacts streaming device makers.
Roku’s hardware losses double despite price increases
The ongoing AI-induced memory chip shortage continues to have a significant impact on consumer hardware makers, including companies in the streaming space. This week, Roku revealed just how massive the problem has become: In its most recent quarter, Roku’s hardware losses more than doubled, jumping from $22.9 million in Q3 of 2025 to $48.6 million.
The company’s hardware gross profit margin was negative 25.1 percent in Q3, which essentially means that the company lost $10 for every $40 streaming stick it sold to consumers.
Granted, that’s oversimplified math not accounting for wholesale revenue cuts as well as a diversified hardware portfolio, but it’s a good rough estimate for how much the company lost selling streaming devices and other hardware through its own website. And it once again shows that RAMageddon has some real consequences for the streaming video industry.
To fully grasp how bad things are, consider this: Roku hiked the prices of its hardware products by up to 60 percent in July , with the price tag of its Roku Ultra streaming box jumping from $100 to a whopping $150. That price increase also showed up in Roku’s Q3 earnings this week, with hardware revenue increasing by 33 percent. In other words: If Roku hadn’t raised its prices, hardware losses would be even more dramatic.
Now, this doesn’t mean that Roku is in trouble. The company has long used hardware as a loss leader, and sold streaming devices at or below cost to increase its user base that then gets monetized through ads and subscriptions. The margin for this part of its business actually increased, and far outweigh any hardware losses. The company’s net income for the quarter was $183.3 million, compared to just $24.8 million a year ago. Total net revenue for the quarter was $1.5 billion.

items.title: NTSB says crucial plane parts found three miles from Florida crash site
items.summary: The NTSB said because the parts were found far from the accident site, they fell off before the crash.
items.content:
Image caption, The NTSB found "the majority" of the Learjet's left elevator - a control surface located on the tail - in three pieces, NTSB member Tom Chapman said
Crucial components of a private jet that crashed in Palm Beach, Florida - including a part that controlled the up-and-down movements of the nose of the plane - were found 1.3 (2 km) to 3.8 miles away from the crash site, an investigator said on Tuesday.
National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigators said they believed parts of the jet may have broken off before the Sunday crash, which killed all nine on board.
The NTSB found "the majority" of the Learjet's left elevator - a control surface on the tail - in three pieces, NTSB board member Tom Chapman said.
Chapman said because the parts were "quite some distance away" from the site, investigators determined they fell off before impact.
Figure caption, Three years before crash, young co-pilot spoke of earning pilot licence
"Knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate," he said.
Chapman said officials were still working out whether losing the left elevator caused the plane to nosedive or whether the part fell off because "forces on the aircraft caused that to separate".
He said the part of the plane that controls upward and downward movement may not have been "effective" at the speed the plane was travelling.
The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas, when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.
In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".
They are then heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
An emergency was declared and the pilots can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
NTSB plans to investigate the role weather played in the crash. Officials were struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on a road in Palm Beach.
Chapman said on Tuesday that the force of the impact severely damaged the wreckage.
Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina, a nanny.
The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory. Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.

DNV Outlook: Energy Security Concerns Drive Pivot Away From Oil and Gas
DNV notes that energy and industrial process-related carbon emissions will have dropped by 2050 by only 44% from today’s level, not even halfway to the net-zero pledge envisioned by the Paris climate agreement.
Supply shocks driven by war in the Middle East and in Ukraine are hastening the decline of fossil fuels in the global energy mix, according to DNV’s Energy Transition Outlook 2026 , which notes that energy security concerns are prompting traditional oil and gas importers to pivot more quickly toward domestically available renewable energy sources.
DNV’s energy transition market forecast through 2060 concluded that near-term concern over energy security is both accelerating the long-term pivot away from oil and gas and causing permanent demand destruction.
“I think that the key theme over the next decade is going to be energy security,” Jason Bedford, visiting senior research fellow, East Asian Institute, National University of Singapore, said during the outlook’s launch event in Singapore in October.
“Every major economy from Japan, Korea, China … everyone is seeking to diversify their sources, including where it is not necessarily cost efficient to do so,” Beford noted. “I don’t see that changing. I think this is a deep structural change in the global energy system.”
In its outlook, DNV forecast that fossil fuels will retain a 51% share of global primary energy supply in 2050. Demand for oil is forecast to decline slowly after peaking in 2028. In contrast, demand for natural gas will remain more buoyant because of the higher cost of alternatives such as hydrogen.
The report notes that “subsurface expertise remains essential, and the long-term runway for gas production remains wide open.”
As for meeting net-zero targets by 2050, DNV notes that energy- and industrial process-related carbon emissions will decline by only 44% by midcentury, falling from 39 gigatons (Gt) today to 22 Gt in 2050, not even halfway to the net-zero pledge envisioned by the Paris climate agreement.
Power generation is expected to lead the way with a 60% reduction in CO 2 emissions, followed by manufacturing at 45% and transport at 34%, with buildings and industrial processes lagging behind. According to the outlook, the slower pace doubles the time expected to achieve net-zero to 2098 and results in a 2.3°C rise temperature increase by 2100.
DNV said global spending on non-fossil energy sources, including renewables and nuclear power, nearly doubled to $1.77 trillion in 2026 from $860 billion in 2021 as major fossil fuel importers such as China, India, and Europe increased the share of non-fossil fuels in their primary energy mix by 2.2 percentage points.
In contrast, fossil fuel exporters such as Russia and countries in the Middle East and North America increased the share of clean energy in their energy mix by only 0.7 percentage points, DNV said.
As oil demand declines, Middle East producers are projected to supply 40% of the world’s oil in 2050, down from the 50% market share projected in DNV’s 2025 Energy Transition Outlook .
Modeling a scenario in which the Middle East conflict continues and oil and gas prices remain elevated through 2030, DNV found “a short-term reduction in demand of 4–6% while the conflict lasts,” along with “a permanent destruction of global oil and gas demand of 2–5% relative to our main forecast through the remainder of our forecast period.”
By 2060, DNV projects global data center and AI electricity demand to reach 5,700 TWh, an increase of 14 times that of current levels. In 30 years, data centers will consume 6.8% of the world’s electricity, compared to 1.2% today, according to the forecast.
Including electricity demand for transportation, such as electric vehicles, and heating increases total power demand from approximately 33,000 TWh to 84,000 TWh by 2060, a 155% rise that DNV forecasts will be met primarily by solar (46%) and wind (31%).
DNV’s model sees a role for natural gas “as a critical transition bridge” to help balance the grid when solar and wind fall short, while nuclear power provides grid stability. It views nuclear as essential in maintaining energy security and predicts global nuclear capacity will grow 30% over the next 10 years and 170% by 2060.
Countries driving electrification tend to be fossil fuel importers exposed to ongoing supply shocks. Electricity demand in Europe, China, and India is projected to increase by an average of 62% over the next 2 decades. In contrast, oil and gas exporters in North America, the Middle East, and Russia are forecast to increase electricity capacity by an average of 47% over the same period.
China is expected to set the pace for electrification, with electricity accounting for 27% of final energy demand today and more than 50% by 2060, DNV said.
China also manufactures more than 80% of the world’s solar modules and 95% of solar wafers, according to International Energy Agency used in the model.

items.content:
Micron or Nvidia: If I Could Only Buy and Hold One of These Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chip Stocks for the Next 5 Years, It Would Be This One
The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has created a generational opportunity for semiconductor companies. As AI hyperscalers like Amazon , Microsoft , Alphabet , and Meta Platforms continue investing in data centers , demand for advanced processors, memory chips, and networking equipment is accelerating.
Two companies are benefiting enormously from this trend: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU). Nvidia dominates the market for graphics processing units (GPUs), while Micron supplies the memory required to power accelerated computing systems.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
While both companies are experiencing remarkable growth, their long-term investment theses are fundamentally different. Micron is capitalizing on an unprecedented shortage of high bandwidth memory (HBM), while Nvidia is quietly transforming into a diversified AI infrastructure and software company.
If I could buy only one of these stocks and hold it through 2030, my choice would be Nvidia. Here's why.
Image source: The Motley Fool. Micron's parabolic growth could eventually become its biggest challenge
Micron's HBM products are essential components for AI accelerators, allowing GPU clusters to process enormous amounts of data quickly and efficiently. As Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices , and other semiconductor companies design more powerful chips, demand for HBM will continue to surge. Meanwhile, Micron's DRAM and NAND memory businesses are benefiting from growing demand across data centers, smartphones, computers, and enterprise storage systems.
During its fiscal fourth quarter of 2026 (ended Sept. 3), Micron generated $54.2 billion in revenue, compared with just $11.3 billion in the same period last year. Net income reached $37.7 billion, while operating cash flow climbed to nearly $44 billion. For the full fiscal year, Micron's revenue increased to approximately $133.2 billion, up 256% year over year.
These figures underscore how dramatically AI is changing the memory market. Importantly, Micron is also expanding production of its HBM4 and HBM4E products, which are designed to support more demanding workloads across agentic AI, robotics, autonomous systems, and other next-generation applications.
Even so, there is a potential problem with Micron's investment thesis. The memory industry is historically cyclical. When demand exceeds available supply, prices rise, allowing manufacturers to generate unusually high profits. In turn, manufacturers invest aggressively in additional production capacity. Eventually, that new capacity catches up with demand, causing prices and profit margins to normalize.
By 2030, Micron could be a substantially larger company while also facing more competition, greater production capacity, and less favorable pricing. This is why I think the company's growth trajectory warrants some caution.
Nvidia's investment thesis is considerably broader than Micron's. During its fiscal second quarter (ended July 26), the company generated $96.2 billion in revenue -- representing 106% year-over-year growth. Its data center business accounted for approximately $89 billion, reflecting ongoing demand for AI compute. However, focusing solely on Nvidia's GPUs misses how the company is expanding.
Consider its partnership with Marvell Technology (NASDAQ: MRVL). In March, Nvidia announced a $2 billion investment in Marvell as part of a strategic collaboration involving custom AI processors, networking technology, and silicon photonics. Through its NVLink Fusion platform, AI developers can integrate specialized chips with Nvidia's broader computing architecture, including CPUs, networking equipment, and rack-scale infrastructure.
This is important because the hyperscalers are developing their own custom processors rather than relying exclusively on general-purpose GPUs. Instead of treating that trend as a competitive threat, Nvidia is positioning itself to participate in the custom-chip ecosystem.
The company is also expanding into telecommunications. Nvidia's $1 billion strategic investment in Nokia (NYSE: NOK) supports the development of AI-powered radio access networks, commonly called AI-RAN. These systems aim to transform traditional telecommunications infrastructure into distributed platforms that support AI applications on edge devices.
Nvidia's ambitions extend beyond hardware. Its CUDA software ecosystem is a major competitive advantage, while platforms such as the Nemotron open AI models are expanding its presence in areas traditionally dominated by frontier model developers like Anthropic and Google DeepMind.
All this means that Nvidia is no longer just selling processors that power AI. The company is increasingly supplying the networking, software, infrastructure, and models that make AI useful.
To me, Nvidia is a more diversified investment opportunity relative to Micron. Micron's profitability remains heavily influenced by the current supply-and-demand imbalance in the memory market.
Sure, Nvidia faces competition and cyclical risks, too. But its growing portfolio of software, networking, custom chips, telecommunications, and open-source models provides several opportunities to generate revenue outside of the core GPU franchise.
On a deeper level, these businesses reinforce one another. A customer deploying Nvidia's GPUs is likely to also purchase its networking equipment, adopt its software tools, and eventually build applications using its AI models. That creates an integrated ecosystem that competitors will struggle to replicate at scale.
While Micron can still deliver impressive upside as long as the memory shortage persists, Nvidia doesn't need a single semiconductor market to remain supply-constrained to succeed in the long run.

Melania Trump to host Ukraine-Russia talks as peace push continues
Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky is set to serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at peace talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Nov. 10-11, Russia confirmed Tuesday.
Separately, first lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss a local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said.
The Kremlin also hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S. and China in the coming days, Russia's Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday.
US First Lady Melania Trump during the Presidential AI Challenge National Champion awards ceremony in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, June 9, 2026.
Russia on Tuesday confirmed that peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. will go ahead next week in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, while also signaling that a meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin , Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to end the conflict was on the table.
Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky will serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at the talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call, according to Reuters.
Separately, first lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss the local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said Tuesday.
Monday saw the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region to allow for evacuation of residents, in a pause of hostilities that the White House said was brokered by the first lady.
KHERSON, UKRAINE - OCTOBER 28: During a ceasefire, a man on a bicycle rides past residential buildings previously damaged by Russian strikes on October 28, 2026 in Kherson, Ukraine. (Photo by Ivan Antypenko/Suspilne Ukraine/JSC "UA:PBC"/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
Global Images Ukraine | Global Images Ukraine | Getty Images
Ukraine on Monday accused Russia of using the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city.
The first lady's summit on Thursday will be "an extraordinary moment in American history," the White House said, but did not name the representatives who will attend. Melania Trump will deliver remarks on the Oleshky ceasefire at 11 a.m. ET on Thursday, it added.
Peskov also said Tuesday the Kremlin hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S. and China in the coming days. The comments follow earlier reports that these countries were planning to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
Zelenskyy has said that any negotiations over Ukraine's future must include Kyiv.
"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said on Oct. 20, adding that he had discussed the proposal of a three-way meeting between the U.S., China and Russia to negotiate an end to the nearly five-year full-scale war. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.

items.title: For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life
items.summary: In Kherson city, usually seething with Russian drones, friends met at cafes, families were out together and shoppers stocked up. "The city seems alive," said one resident, "just like it used to be."
items.content:
Ceasefire ends in Ukraine's Kherson region In Kherson city, usually seething with Russian drones, friends met at cafes, families were out together and shoppers stocked up. "The city seems alive," said one resident, "just like it used to be."
For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life
A brief ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region has ended
< iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-151238/nx-s1-9988884" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
People walk past the destroyed location of a cafe in Kherson, Ukraine.
KHERSON, Ukraine — In this city where Russian drones usually fill the skies, Olena Soboleva could not easily walk down the street to meet her best friend, Anna Herasimenko.
Then came last week's truce, negotiated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, in a corner of southern Ukraine that included Kherson.
This weekend, the two friends, both 21, took the opportunity to venture outside to autumnal skies clear of drones and guided bombs.
Best friends Anna Herasimenko and Olena Soboleva, both 21, spent the ceasefire taking walks in the city and having coffee at a favorite cafe. They rarely see each other in person because constant drone attacks make it too dangerous to venture outside.
"No drones, no explosions," Soboleva says. "No one wants to kill you."
They passed families strolling with their kids, shoppers stocking up on supplies and couples holding hands. They lined up at a cafe filled with paintings of cats.
"The city seems alive," says Herasimenko, "just like it used to be."
Over the weekend, she had also ventured to a salon.
"I did my nails," she says, showing off fresh burgundy polish. "The streets are full of people, just as they were in the past."
The truce ended Sunday night. Russia and Ukraine agreed to it in order to help Oleshky, a town across the Dnipro River from Kherson. Russian troops occupied Oleshky in 2022 and mined the land around it. Food and medicine rarely got through. NPR spoke to the families of residents there, who said their loved ones survived on pickles and boiled weeds.
Over the weekend, hundreds of Oleshky residents were evacuated, eventually escorted into northern Ukraine on buses. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's ombudsman — the country's independent watchdog for human rights — thanked Melania Trump for ensuring that the ceasefire, which lasted from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1, happened.
Residents of Kherson walk into a bus at a busy public transit stop on Nov. 1, the last day of the local ceasefire.
A woman walks past a public bus in Kherson during the ceasefire.
Kherson residents wait for public buses under drone nets during the last days of a local ceasefire in southern Ukraine.
"I believe they can be upheld and honored," Lubinets said about truces between Ukraine and Russia.
Even a short pause in hostilities was a respite for Kherson. Russian troops occupied the city for several months in 2022, until local partisans spied for Ukrainian soldiers, who then forced the Russians out of the city.
Anti-drone nets protect the road leading into Kherson, Ukraine.
Workers repair tunnels of heavyweight mesh mesh nets that protect a highway leading into the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson from Russian FPV (first-person-view) drone attacks.
Locals walk through Independence Square in the center of Kherson, Ukraine, where a short local ceasefire offered respite from constant drone attacks.
Since 2024, Russian troops based across the river have hunted Kherson residents with FPV (first-person-view) drones strapped with explosives. The highway into Kherson is shrouded in tunnels of heavy mesh nets to protect locals from these drones. These anti-drone nets also cover Kherson's streets and many of its buildings.
This weekend, cars pulled up next to the Greek-style monument marking the city's gateway.
Svitlana Vorobiova, a retired police officer, drove here from a safer city where she now lives. She took photos with her children at the monument.
A boy poses for a photo at the entrance to the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson. Families who fled Kherson because of Russia's constant bomb and drone attacks on the city returned during the days of a short ceasefire that ended Nov. 1.
Svitlana Vorobiova, a retired police officer from Kherson, Ukraine, is emotional as she returns home during a ceasefire that ended Nov. 1.
"I have a place in Kherson, and my parents are also here," she says, and her voice breaks. Tears fill her eyes.
"I brought my son with me," Vorobiova says. "He hasn't been here in four years. He said, 'I cannot believe I'm in my hometown!'"
Inside the city, Volodymyr Mykolaienko, a former mayor of Kherson, strolls past the crushed remains of a once-grand administrative building. Locals stop him and shake his hand. He says he's happy to see so many people outside.
"I walk around the city a lot these days," he says. "I cannot sit still at home."
A shopper passes the central market in Kherson during a short ceasefire. Locals stocked up on groceries as the truce kept skies clear of Russian FPV (first-person-view) drones that often target civilians in the city.
Women at a market in Kherson during a local ceasefire that ended Nov. 1.
Volodymyr Mykolaienko, a former mayor of Kherson, stands in Independence Square in the city. He spent most of Russia's full-scale assault on Ukraine as a prisoner of war in Russia. He was arrested while Kherson was under Russian occupation in 2022. Ukrainian troops liberated the city in November 2022, and Mykolaienko was released in a prisoner exchange last year.
Mykolaienko, 66, spent years as a prisoner of war in Russia, confined to tiny rooms, starved and tortured. Russian troops arrested him in Kherson in early 2022, when the city was under Russian occupation. Mykolaienko was freed last year in a prisoner exchange and returned to Kherson, where his family still lives.
This truce allowed him to visit his father's grave. The cemetery is in a part of the city that's usually filled with drones.
"I could not hold myself back," he says. "I was able to do exactly what I have long wanted to do — to talk to my father, pray, thank him for my life and to tell him what was happening to our city."
Olena Yehorova, an oncology nurse, on the bus during the last days of the ceasefire in Kherson, Ukraine.
At a busy bus stop, oncology nurse Olena Yehorova smiles at a gray-haired man playing folk music on his accordion.
"This truce has been such a relief," she says. "The people in our city have been able to breathe. Of course, we still walk around with caution, because you cannot trust the Russians."
She couldn't help looking up at the sky. A few hours later, the truce was over. She said she expects new attacks to resume at any time.
NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this report from Kyiv.

items.content:
Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia he operation involved a warship, a maritime surveillance aircraft and marine commandos. The hijacking followed a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.
Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
FILE - Fishermen stand on the Indian Ocean beach at dusk in the former pirate village of Eyl, in Somalia's semiautonomous northeastern state of Puntland, Somalia, March 6, 2017.
MOGADISHU, Somalia — Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat and its crew of 20 hijacked off Somalia after an operation lasting more than 48 hours, India's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The rescue of the Azini was completed Monday in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said.
An official with the Puntland Maritime Police Force told The Associated Press that Indian forces disarmed 12 suspected Somali pirates, confiscated their mobile phones and released them. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.
The suspects and two Somali security guards later came ashore at Bandar Bayla in northeastern Somalia, the official said. Three of those who came ashore had minor injuries, but he did not specify whether they were suspects or guards, or how they were hurt.
India's ministry said the operation ended without casualties or injuries. It did not specify whether that account covered everyone aboard or only the rescued crew. It was unclear whether the crew remained on the vessel or were moved elsewhere.
The operation involved a warship, a maritime surveillance aircraft and marine commandos. An Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft airdropped additional commandos, the ministry said.
The Azini was hijacked Oct. 29 between Bandar Bayla and Hafun. A Puntland maritime police officer said on Sunday that it carried 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. The difference between that crew count and India's rescue figure could not immediately be explained.
Indian forces tracked the vessel by sea and air before securing it, the ministry said. It said there had been concern that pirates could use the boat as a floating base for attacks on commercial ships.
The Puntland official said regional authorities learned of the rescue only after it had taken place.
The hijacking followed a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. By August, pirates had hijacked six commercial vessels since April, some far from Somalia's coast. They included the oil products tanker Sibu 1, seized about 252 kilometers (136 nautical miles) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen.
In September, Puntland authorities said pirates killed five crew members of the tanker MT Honour 25 before security forces recovered it. The tanker had been held since April. Authorities said they detained 16 suspected pirates.
The renewed piracy adds to shipping risks in a region already disrupted by the Iran war. Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and threats by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb have complicated oil transport routes.
Those disruptions have lengthened voyages and driven up tanker costs. Some oil shipments diverted around Africa face journeys up to a month longer.
International naval patrols and improved maritime security have sharply reduced Somali piracy over the past decade, but recent hijackings have renewed concerns about the threat.

items.title: No more rice grains in Kellogg's Rice Krispies due to changing weather
items.summary: The new recipes mean cereal packaging will now include a 'contains wheat gluten' warning.
items.content:
Breakfast cereal giant Kellogg's has stopped using rice grains in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops in the UK due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies.
Corn flour and rice flour are being used instead, a Kellogg's spokesperson said on Tuesday, adding that the updated recipes have been "carefully assessed" and the firm has taken customer feedback into consideration.
Those ingredients are replacing rice grains as crops have been hit by dry weather in key producing countries in Asia, reducing harvests and driving up prices.
The new recipes mean cereal packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning.
Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada will continue to be made with real rice with no changes to their recipes expected, a spokesperson for Kellogg's North American business told the BBC.
The recipe change in the UK will help "maintain consistent quality at a time when changing weather conditions are affecting the quality and availability of some of the rice and grains used in our cereals," a Kellogg's spokesperson told the BBC.
"We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration."
The company also said that Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food.
The cereals also contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same, the spokesperson added.
The Kellogg company separated into two distinct firms in 2023.
The largest is Kellanova, which focuses on snacks, cereals, noodles and other food products like Eggo, Pringles and Pop-Tarts sold globally. It is now owned by Mars, which makes confectionery and pet food.
